technique.how: Establish exactly when consciousness was lost relative to activity: during ongoing exertion (walking uphill, running, lifting) versus in the minutes after stopping. Ask what the patient was doing, whether there were palpitations or chest pain first, and whether a witness saw the collapse mid-activity.
technique.prerequisites: Patient or witness account; clarify timing precisely because post-exertional collapse is usually reflex.

interpretation.positive_finding: Syncope during exertion is uncommon but highly specific for a cardiac cause (pooled LR+ ~7; specificity 98-99%) and should prompt evaluation for aortic stenosis, HCM, ischemia, or ventricular arrhythmia before any return to activity.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of exertional syncope barely changes the probability of cardiac syncope (LR- ~0.9) because only ~13% of cardiac syncope is exertional.
interpretation.pitfalls: Collapse immediately after stopping exercise is typically reflex (post-exertional vasovagal) and must be distinguished from mid-exertion syncope; patients may not recall the exact timing. Exertional syncope is rare, so its absence is not reassuring.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: admit/monitor, ECG plus echocardiogram and cardiology review before discharge; negative: no change in workup.

estimates.population: Pooled derivation sample from 2 studies (Alboni 2001, Del Rosso 2008) reporting syncope during effort in adults with syncope
estimates.reference_standard: Final adjudicated cause of syncope in each primary study (cardiac vs non-cardiac)
estimates.computed_from: Cardiac: 16 effort syncope / 122 (13%); non-cardiac: 9 / 475 (2%). LR+ = 0.131/0.019 = 6.92 (table reports 6.92); LR- = 0.869/0.981 = 0.89.
estimates.location: Table 2, 'Syncope during effort' row (PMC3815402 full text)

estimates.population: 261 consecutive patients aged >=65 y with unexplained syncope referred to secondary/tertiary hospitals (34% cardiac)
estimates.reference_standard: Pre-specified ESC-based diagnostic criteria for cause of syncope
estimates.quote: Myoclonic movements, effort syncope, and supine position during loss of consciousness were the most specific (97%, 99%, and 99%, respectively) diagnostic criteria

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not classify as non-exertional (reassuring) when timing is uncertain; treat ambiguous timing as exertional until echo/ECG are reviewed.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Exertional syncope with a murmur, family history of sudden death, chest pain, or abnormal ECG is a red flag for AS/HCM/VT: no discharge without cardiology evaluation.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Depends on precise history of timing relative to activity; definitions of 'effort' differ between studies.

extraction_notes: Estimate 0 computed from pooled 2x2 counts in Table 2 of Berecki-Gisolf 2013 (PMC3815402 open-access XML dump); the table's LR column (6.92) matches the computed LR+, LR- computed by me. Only two derivation studies contributed effort data (Alboni 2001 and Del Rosso 2008), so this is a small pooled sample. Estimate 1: Del Rosso 2005 (PubMed year 2006), older patients only: specificity 99% for effort syncope; sensitivity not in abstract (abstract notes all three specific features together accounted for only 14% of patients). Albassam 2019 RCE abstract does not report an exertion-specific LR (not visible without full text), cited as context. Alboni 2001 abstract names 'during effort' among the most specific predictors in patients with heart disease but gives no number; EGSYS abstract lists 'syncope during effort' as a score item without per-item accuracy. Quote 0 is a contiguous 25-word span of the table row.
